Update · Thursday, June 11 — Week One in the Books

We published this preview before release with BCM v2.1's opening calls. Week one is now complete — here's the full ledger through Wednesday, and an honest grade on where our model was sharp and where it slipped. The interesting part: we missed in both directions.

  • Peddi — we called ₹100.5 Cr weekend / ₹170 Cr net. The weekend ran hot; the week ran cold.
    Day-by-day net (Sacnilk): previews ₹18.50 · Thu ₹51.00 · Fri ₹26.90 · Sat ₹29.10 · Sun ₹32.15 · Mon ₹12.35 · Tue ₹9.70 · Wed ₹7.55. The 3-day weekend landed ~₹88 Cr (we said ₹100.5 — BCM over-priced Saturday, ₹38 modeled vs ₹29 actual, with reviews and the Janhvi Kapoor controversy capping the bump). But the full-week net hit ₹187.25 Cr — above our ₹170 call — on a monster ₹51 Cr Day 1 and steadier weekday holds than we modeled. WW gross past ₹277 Cr; it overtook Bhooth Bangla's entire lifetime in seven days. Verdict: weekend over-modeled, total under-called. A hit.
  • Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai — we called ₹31 Cr. The weekend did ~₹24 Cr; week one closed at ₹36.34 Cr. Day 1 (₹7.50 Cr) sat in our band, but Saturday stayed flat (₹7.50 Cr) instead of climbing, and the weekdays faded to ₹2.19 Cr by Thursday. It edged Baby John's ₹32.65 Cr first week but fell short of Sunny Sanskari Ki Tulsi Kumari's ₹38.85 Cr. Verdict: ran hot ~₹7 Cr on the weekend; a disappointment overall.
  • Bandar — we called ₹2.4 Cr; it did ~₹1.96 Cr. Bobby Deol drew the best reviews of his recent career, but the footfall never followed and it stayed niche through the week. Verdict: on-model.
  • Obsession — we treated it as a modest ~₹4.5 Cr holdover. It became the breakout of the season. Its India total now stands at ₹47.32 Cr gross (~₹40 Cr net, Sacnilk), and its second weekend (₹17.55 Cr net) almost matched its entire first week — a ~125% jump that is all but unheard of for a non-franchise horror release. It has passed The Devil Wears Prada 2 (₹28 Cr) to sit among the top five Hollywood horror films ever in India and is chasing Michael (₹65 Cr) for 2026's biggest Hollywood release here. Worldwide it has crossed $200M — Focus Features' highest-grossing film ever, on a sub-$1M budget. Verdict: we under-called it — the word-of-mouth breakout BCM never saw coming.

The honest lesson, two ways: BCM v2.1 over-weighted the Saturday advance bump (too hot on the weekend peak), but on a star-driven Telugu vehicle like Peddi it under-weighted opening-day pull and weekday durability (too cold on the total). We're doing both fixes ahead of next week's INCU run — trimming the Saturday-growth coefficient, lifting the weekday-hold curve for big Telugu releases, and — after Obsession — building a word-of-mouth surge signal so a second weekend can climb, not just decay. That's the whole point of grading ourselves in public.

Editor's note Back at the desk, and the timing's almost too on-the-nose. This is the single busiest weekend on the 2026 calendar: a real pan-India event film, two Hindi releases carrying an industry's nerves, a pile of holdovers that won't quit, and a Hollywood story odd enough to end up in a textbook. Grab a chai. Let's get into it.

For five months, the 2026 box office has had a shape: the South builds blockbusters, Hollywood occasionally detonates, and Bollywood waits for a hit that mostly doesn't arrive. This weekend compresses all three storylines into one frame. Peddi is the event. Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai and Bandar are the test. Obsession is the anomaly nobody scripted. The opening numbers will be loud — but the real story is which of these films still matters on Monday.

I.The Event

Peddi Opens Into a ₹350 Crore Hole — and the Opening Is the Easy Part

Posters auto-load from TMDB on page-load · the three new releases of the weekend

Buchi Babu Sana — the writer-director who turned Uppena into a phenomenon — has spent two years building Peddi, a sports action drama set in 1980s rural Andhra Pradesh, with A.R. Rahman on the score and Ram Charan in what early viewers are calling a career-best performance. The first reviews land around a measured three-out-of-five: real praise for Ram Charan and the craft, real reservations about length (189 minutes) and the back half. That gap between "his best act" and "three stars" is the whole ballgame.

The advance backs that up. ₹20.66 crore in India pre-sales across languages by Thursday morning is a top-tier Telugu number, and films this size usually double it once spot bookings and the benefit shows are counted. So yes, the opening will be enormous. The harder question — the one nobody at the trailer launch wanted to say out loud — is what "enormous" actually has to beat when the budget is reported at ₹350 crore.

North America: a $1M+ premiere into the summer's most crowded screen-crush

Overseas is where Peddi is really flexing. It cleared $100K in North American pre-sales within four hours of bookings opening — the fastest any Indian film has ever done that — and premiere advances have since climbed past $1.1 million, about 77% of what Game Changer pulled for its premiere. The premium screens are doing a lot of the lifting: XD, RPX, D-Box and the other PLF formats account for nearly $280K of the US presale on their own, with Cinemark leading the chains. Add Day 1 and the premieres are tracking toward roughly $2 million. It's a big start, and it needs to be one: the all-language North American break-even sits near $6.5 million, and the full overseas figure is closer to $9 million.

But here's the catch the presale numbers don't show. Peddi is opening into the most congested premium-screen weekend Hollywood has all summer. Two new studio films land the same Friday, and two horror hits from the past month aren't giving their auditoriums back.

None of those four chases Peddi's audience — but they are chasing the same premium auditoriums. With Scary Movie 6 and He-Man flooding 3,400–3,500 sites and two horror holdovers refusing to thin out, Peddi's overseas showtimes in PLF formats will be tighter than its presale momentum deserves. The presale is elite; the screen availability is the variable.

The verdict math: why the opening tells you almost nothing

On a ₹350 crore budget, the verdict ladder turns brutal. Sit with this one for a second.

VerdictBudget multipleWorldwide gross requiredReference point
Disaster< 0.5×< ₹175 CrCatastrophic
Flop0.5–1×₹175–350 CrGame Changer territory
Below Average1–1.5×₹350–525 CrRecoups, no profit
Average1.5–2×₹525–700 CrModest win
Plus2–2.5×₹700–875 CrHit-adjacent
Hit2.5–3×₹875–1,050 CrNeeds RRR-scale legs
Super Hit3–5×₹1,050–1,750 CrPushpa 2 zone
Blockbuster5–7×₹1,750–2,450 CrGenerational

Peddi needs something like ₹875 crore worldwide just to be called a Hit, a number Ram Charan has reached exactly once, and that was inside the RRR ensemble. Game Changer opened to roughly ₹51 crore on Day 1 last year and still ended up a flop, simply because the base underneath it was too big to ever satisfy. That's the whole point here: the opening weekend will tell us almost nothing about Peddi's verdict. The second-week hold and the overseas legs will tell us everything.

The Boxoffy Take
Peddi will post a monster opening and a chunk of the trade will declare victory by Saturday night. Ignore it. This film's verdict lives in the ₹350 crore budget line, and on that scale a brilliant opening that drops 55% in week two is a flop with a press release. Watch the Monday-to-Thursday hold and the North American number — that's where Game Changer quietly died, and where Peddi has to prove it's different.

II.Bollywood's Referendum

Two Hindi Films, One Drought, Zero Margin for Error

Here is the uncomfortable fact framing every Hindi release in June. Through five months of 2026, only three Hindi films have been box office successes — Border 2, Dhurandhar 2 and Bhooth Bangla — and nothing has clicked since Bhooth Bangla. Across May, six notable Hindi releases combined for roughly ₹100 crore net between them. That is not a slump; that is a structural confidence problem. Into it walk two films that could not be more different.

And they walk in with one hand tied. With Peddi commanding the lion's share of high-capacity shows nationwide — prime evening multiplex slots and most premium screens in the South and metros — both Hindi films open on visibly constrained showtime counts. In a normal week HJTIHH would headline the Friday grid; this week it shares it with a ₹350 crore juggernaut. Screen count, not just word-of-mouth, is a live variable for both.

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai — a comfort-food bet with a farewell attached

This is the David Dhawan playbook, undisguised: Varun Dhawan, a love triangle with Pooja Hegde and Mrunal Thakur, remixed 90s hits (a reworked Chunari Chunari), slapstick, and the warm familiarity of a brand that printed money in the 2000s. But there's a weight to it this time the box office models miss — David Dhawan has announced that this, his 46th film, is his last. Karan Johar wrote an emotional tribute calling him "an institution… responsible for creating an entire genre"; Anupam Kher publicly "scolded" him for retiring. This is the swan song of the man who built Hindi commercial comedy, and that narrative is real promotional fuel for the back half of the weekend.

The encouraging part is the comparison. The closest profile on the board is Pati Patni aur Woh Do, a mid-budget Hindi entertainer that opened modestly and then refused to fall off, legging its way to around ₹55 crore net. HJTIHH fits that same mould, and its advance is running ahead of where the doubters put it: 20,000+ Day 1 tickets sold with a day still on the clock. David Dhawan's last theatrical hit with Varun was Judwaa 2, nine years back, so nobody should pencil this in as an event. But a soft open that compounds on family word-of-mouth across Saturday and Sunday, with the farewell story doing the rest, is a very real route to a quiet success in a market that badly needs one.

Bandar — the prestige swing

Bobby Deol's first film with Anurag Kashyap, fresh off a TIFF 2025 world premiere, with Sanya Malhotra and Saba Azad in the ensemble and Zee Studios behind it. A gritty, layered drama about a fading artist whose world unravels — this is not a Day 1 number, it's a reviews-and-festivals play that lives or dies on critic reception and metro multiplex word-of-mouth. Bobby Deol is in a full-blown career renaissance as a character actor; Kashyap is Kashyap. If the reviews are strong, Bandar can have a long, quiet, profitable life on a small base. It is the opposite risk profile to HJTIHH.

The Boxoffy Take
Neither film is built to "save" Bollywood this weekend, and judging them on that bar is unfair. HJTIHH's job is the Pati Patni aur Woh Do job: open reasonably — ₹7–10 crore — and then hold, letting family word-of-mouth and the David Dhawan farewell compound the number through Sunday and beyond. Bandar's job is simply to be good; a strong review cycle is worth more to its economics than a big Friday. And the film actually eating Hindi screens this weekend isn't either of them — it's Peddi, in every language including the dub.

Karuppu is the cleanest story of the three. Suriya's action-drama sits at ₹297 crore worldwide and should join the ₹300 crore club over the weekend — a real milestone for Kollywood, even with fresh Tamil and Malayalam titles starting to nibble at its screens. Deool Band 2, almost without anyone noticing, became just the second Marathi film of 2026 to cross ₹50 crore.

IV.The Anomaly

Obsession Refuses to Behave Like a Box Office Movie

Every so often a film breaks the rules so completely that the rules look silly. Obsession — Curry Barker's R-rated horror thriller from Focus Features, made for roughly $750,000 — is that film. As of June 3 it has grossed about $166 million worldwide ($121.8M domestic, ~$45M overseas). The micro-budget-to-gross ratio is not a typo: roughly a 220× return at the worldwide level, before ancillaries.

FrameWeekend gross (US)What it means
Weekend 1$17.2MSolid genre open from 2,615 theaters
Weekend 2$23.0MGrew +34% — almost never happens
Weekend 3$26.4MGrew again — beat its own opening

A wide release that makes more money in its third weekend than its first is the sort of thing that gets E.T. dragged into the conversation. This is word-of-mouth compounding in real time. There's no franchise here and no stars; the theatre count is simply expanding to chase demand instead of front-loading it. And it pulled this off while A24's record-smashing Backrooms ($81.4M, the biggest original-horror debut ever) opened right on top of it. Obsession held anyway. Then it grew.

~220×
Obsession's worldwide gross vs. its ~$750K budget — among the great ROI stories in modern horror, and the clearest sign yet that a great hook plus organic momentum can out-earn a marketing budget.

The India angle — and the censor's scissors

What's quietly remarkable is the India run. A starless American horror film with zero local marketing muscle has crossed ₹15.26 crore net through Day 6 and is still adding — Day 6 alone brought in ₹2.51 crore on a holding curve, not a collapsing one. Plenty of mid-budget Hindi films this year never got near that figure. It's the clearest sign yet that the Indian audience's appetite for horror now extends to subtitled, no-star Hollywood horror when the word-of-mouth is strong enough.

And it's doing all of this handicapped. Despite an adults-only 'A' certificate, the CBFC ordered 38 seconds of cuts before release — 24 seconds trimmed from a key extreme-violence sequence in the second half and a 14-second sex scene removed entirely. Horror fans erupted online, many complaining the edits broke the flow and gutted a crucial stretch of the story; "a significant portion of the storyline was lost," as one viewer put it. The remarkable part: it didn't matter to the box office. A film that arrived in India pre-trimmed, with its most-discussed scenes blunted, still out-held most of the local slate. That's what a true word-of-mouth phenomenon looks like.

The Boxoffy Take
Obsession is the most important small film of the year, and not because of the dollar figure. It's a proof of concept: in 2026, a great hook plus organic social momentum can out-earn a marketing budget — and the appetite reaches all the way to Indian multiplexes, scissors and all. Studios spent the decade learning to manufacture opening weekends. Obsession just demonstrated the audience can still manufacture a second and third one on its own.

The thing that would surprise us: if Peddi's reviews convert into RRR-style positive word-of-mouth, the ₹350 crore math becomes survivable and the conversation changes overnight. The thing we expect: a huge Peddi opening, a respectable-not-revolutionary HJTIHH that leans on legs and the David Dhawan farewell, a critically warm Bandar on a small base, and Karuppu quietly stepping into the ₹300 crore club while everyone watches the new arrivals.

The signal under the noise: three of the four biggest stories this weekend — Peddi, Karuppu, Drishyam 3 — are South Indian, and the fourth is American horror. Bollywood's two entries are framed not as events but as tests. That sentence is the 2026 box office in miniature, and June is the month it either changes or hardens.

VI.The OTT Pulse

While Theatres Fight, the Year's Biggest Film Quietly Switches Screens

There's a second box office story running underneath this weekend, and it's a big one. The same Friday Peddi storms cinemas, the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year — Dhurandhar 2 — lands on streaming as Dhurandhar: The Revenge (Raw & Undekha), an extended, uncensored cut on JioHotstar with footage that never cleared theatrical certification. A ₹1,000 crore+ theatrical phenomenon converting to a living-room event the same weekend a new ₹350 crore one opens is the whole theatrical-vs-streaming tension of 2026 in a single grid.

The Weekend In Summary
The Opening Is the Question. The Hold Is the Answer.
By Saturday night the trade will have crowned Peddi, written off one of the Hindi films, and moved on. Don't. This weekend's verdict isn't written on Friday — it's written next Wednesday, in the second-week holds, the overseas adds, and whether word-of-mouth compounds the way it did for a $750,000 horror film nobody marketed. Peddi has a ₹350 crore hole to climb out of; David Dhawan has a career to close on the right note; and a censored micro-budget horror is quietly out-holding films a thousand times its size. We'll be back with the Weekend Recap once the actuals land.
